01

Hashing

A tamper-evident fingerprint for data — change one letter, get an unrecognizable result.

Photo: Simon A. Eugster (LivingShadow) / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0

Topic 01 — Hashing

Four properties that make it work

Deterministic

The same input always produces the exact same output — hash "hello" today or in ten years, identical result.

One-Way

Given a hash, there's no way back to the original input — like a wax seal you can't un-melt into the letter.

Avalanche Effect

Change one character of the input, and the entire output becomes unrecognizable — no partial resemblance.

Collision-Resistant

Practically impossible to find two different inputs that produce the same hash.

Worked Example — Real Output

One flipped letter, zero resemblance

$ echo -n "Send 1 ETH to Alice" | shasum -a 256
9bed087e0a716e203d57c1ba36493085f7a87628da1cb1fe18bf5b4631bd7e45

$ echo -n "Send 1 ETH to Alicf" | shasum -a 256
94f17d20a09db58f6a7fe2cf97f00b2ae2dc1a67802b6e74776b0b6785e4b1eb
# one letter changed: e → f. total mismatch.

Real-World Uses

Not just blockchain

Software checksums Git version control Password storage Cloud dedup Digital forensics Certificate Transparency

Full explanations, plus a runnable script, live in curriculum/week-01/01-hashing.md

02

Public / Private Keys

Prove ownership without ever revealing the secret that proves it.

Photo: Shillings1005 / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0

Topic 02 — Public / Private Keys

Two keys, two different jobs

Private Key

A secret number that signs transactions. Never leaves your device, never shared.

Public Key

Derived one-way from the private key. Safe to share — can't be reversed back to the secret.

Signature

Proof you hold the private key, produced without ever revealing it.

Address

A hash of the public key — one more one-way step, for extra safety margin.

Important distinction: blockchain wallets mostly use signing (proving authorship), not encryption (hiding content) — every transaction detail is public, only authorization is proven.

Worked Example — Real Keypair

Generated with openssl, secp256k1

$ openssl dgst -sha256 -verify pub.pem \
  -signature sig.bin message.txt
Verified OK

$ # same signature, tampered message:
$ openssl dgst -sha256 -verify pub.pem \
  -signature sig.bin tampered.txt
Verification failure

Real-World Uses

You already use this daily

HTTPS / TLS SSH keys Code signing Signed git commits PGP email

The padlock icon in your browser right now is running this exact math. Full walkthrough in 02-public-private-keys.md

03

Blocks & Chains

Link history together so a single altered link breaks everything after it.

Photo: Petritap / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0

Topic 03 — Blocks & Chains

Anatomy of a block

Timestamp

When the block was created.

Previous Hash

The literal link to the block before it.

Transactions

The batch of data this block records.

Own Hash

Computed from everything above — including the previous hash.

Because of the avalanche effect (Topic 01), editing an old block changes its hash — which breaks every block chained after it. That's the entire trick.

Worked Example — A Real Tampering Attempt

You already use this structure — it's called Git

# 3-block chain, attacker edits block 2:
Block 2 original hash:
7dd7f6149021fd74...23f
Block 3 still expects prev =
7dd7f6149021fd74...23f

Block 2 hash AFTER edit:
6c7db182ce1b8061...216
Match? False
# real output, real git repo:
$ git log --format="commit %H%nparent %P"

commit 14170b8693832cd8...4361
parent 5c0144c7a07feca6...1304

commit 5c0144c7a07feca6...1304
parent  (none — first commit)

Every commit you've ever made stores its parent's hash. Full walkthrough, plus block-explorer practice, in 03-blockchain-viewing.md

04

Consensus

How thousands of strangers agree on one shared truth, with no referee.

Photo: Carl Lender / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0

Topic 04 — Consensus

Two answers to the same problem

Proof of Work

Miners burn real electricity solving a puzzle. Hard to solve, instant to verify. Cheating wastes your own money.

Proof of Stake

Validators lock up currency as collateral. Cheating gets that collateral destroyed ("slashed").

Ethereum switched from PoW to PoS in September 2022. Same underlying goal — the honest-majority Byzantine Generals Problem — two different economic answers.

Consensus, By The Numbers

Real math, real incidents

n ≥ 3f + 1

The fault-tolerance rule: honest nodes must outnumber dishonest ones more than 2-to-1.

32 ETH

Locked as collateral per validator to propose Ethereum blocks under Proof of Stake.

$10.1M

Double-spent across Ethereum Classic's three confirmed 51%-attacks — Jan 2019, Jul & Aug 2020. A real, documented case, not a hypothetical.

Same problem, other rooms: Kubernetes' etcd (Raft) · CockroachDB / Spanner (Paxos) · aircraft flight-control redundancy — the original 1982 motivation for Byzantine fault tolerance research.
